Use case 01 — Exhaled VOCs before and after biologics in severe asthma

Reproducing Vassileva et al., Respir Med 2026;262:109067 with the DMP-AE skills, on synthetic data

11 October 2026

1 What this notebook is

This is a worked use case for the 3TR DMP Analytical Engine. It walks through the full analysis in

Vassileva SM, Shahbazi Khamas S, et al. The impact of benralizumab and dupilumab on exhaled volatile organic compound profiles of severe asthma patients – a preliminary analysis. Respiratory Medicine 262 (2026) 109067. doi:10.1016/j.rmed.2026.109067

and runs each step with the engine’s skills (R scripts under .claude/skills/). The same steps can be run one by one through the MCP server or by asking Claude.

The data are synthetic. The 3TR-ABC breath data are available only on request, so data/simulate_breath_data.R generates a cohort with the same design and with known (“planted”) effects. Numbers below describe the simulation, not the 3TR-ABC cohort. The point is the workflow: how to reproduce the methods, what the outputs look like, and how to check them.

2 Synthetic cohort

if (!file.exists(file.path(UC, "data", "metadata.csv")) || isTRUE(params$rerun)) {
  skill(file.path(UC, "data", "simulate_breath_data.R"), c(file.path(UC, "data"), params$seed))
}
meta  <- utils::read.csv(file.path(UC, "data", "metadata.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
truth <- utils::read.csv(file.path(UC, "data", "planted_truth.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
addmargins(table(biologic = meta$biologic, visit = factor(meta$visit, c("BL", "M1", "M4"))))
##               visit
## biologic       BL M1 M4 Sum
##   benralizumab  5  2  5  12
##   dupilumab    20 13 20  53
##   Sum          25 15 25  65

The generator mirrors the paper’s design. It has 25 patients from two sites; 20 started dupilumab and 5 benralizumab. Breath was sampled at baseline (BL) and 4 months (M4) for everyone, and at 1 month (M1) for 15 patients. Each sample has 4,270 GC-MS ion fragments, of which 1,062 are known contaminants, and samples were run in four GC-MS batches. These effects are planted:

kt(head(truth[truth$type != "time_effect_background", ], 7))
feature compound type effect_log_M4_vs_BL
MZ052_RT0496 methyl isobutyl ketone time_effect -0.80
MZ039_RT0933 2-ethyl-1-hexanol time_effect 0.80
MZ098_RT1193 5-methyloctadecane time_effect -0.75
MZ104_RT1080 2-methylundecane time_effect -0.75
MZ141_RT1143 1,1’-oxybis(decane) time_effect -0.75
MZ039_RT0933 2-ethyl-1-hexanol baseline_trait: + ACQ-5 NA
MZ141_RT1143 1,1’-oxybis(decane) baseline_trait: - blood eosinophils NA

Fifteen weaker, unnamed time-responsive fragments are also planted. Every planted VOC responds in about 80% of patients; the rest is noise. The two baseline traits are constant within each patient. The multilevel model cannot see them, but the baseline correlations should.

  n = c(sum(w$acq5.BL - w$acq5.M4 >= 0.5), sum(w$acq5.M4 < 1.5), sum(w$fev1_pp.M4 - w$fev1_pp.BL >= 10)),

The paper’s “≥10%” FEV1 improvement could mean percentage points or a relative change; percentage points are used here.

6 GC-MS preprocessing (Methods 2.5, Suppl. Fig. 1)

The paper’s processing order is: XCMS → contaminant removal → log transform → z-score → PCA to check batch → limma batch correction. The engine starts from the aligned XCMS table, because raw chromatograms are not part of the data contract.

skill(file.path(K, "prep-breathomics-gcms/scripts/breath_preprocess.R"),
      c(paste0("--config=", CFG), "--layer=breath_voc"),
      done = file.path(RES, "data/breath_voc_processed_se.rds"), show = 0)

As in the paper, 4,270 fragments go in and 3,208 remain after contaminant removal. Batch correction removes the batch structure from the leading PCs. Here batches are nested within site, so the correction also removes site differences; the QC file flags this.

7 Multilevel sPLS-DA: baseline vs 4 months (Fig. 3, Table 2)

The paper’s model, with its settings:

  • fragments z-scored, multilevel decomposition (within-patient variation only);
  • sPLS-DA with keepX tuned, then stepwise backward elimination: a feature is kept only if removing it drops the AUC by more than 5%, with a target AUC of about 0.9;
  • AUROC of the final model on the full data, then leave-one-subject-out CV with the panel fixed.

The skill also adds a nested cross-validation, which repeats tuning and elimination inside every outer fold (patient-grouped 5-fold × 5 repeats), and a within-patient permutation null. These are the checks the paper’s design needs.

run <- "splsda/BLvsM4_breath_voc"
skill(file.path(K, "ml-multilevel-splsda/scripts/multilevel_splsda.R"),
      c(paste0("--config=", CFG), "--layer=breath_voc", "--visits=BL,M4",
        "--drop_max=0.05", "--target_auc=0.9", "--elim_auc=train",
        paste0("--n_perm=", params$n_perm), "--plot_visits=BL,M1,M4", "--colour_by=biologic"),
      done = file.path(RES, run, "performance.csv"), show = 0)
## $ Rscript .claude/skills/ml-multilevel-splsda/scripts/multilevel_splsda.R --config=usecases/01_breathomics_biologics/study_config.json --layer=breath_voc --visits=BL,M4 --drop_max=0.05 --target_auc=0.9 --elim_auc=train --n_perm=20 --plot_visits=BL,M1,M4 --colour_by=biologic
tun <- rd(run, "tuning.csv"); el <- rd(run, "elimination_log.csv")
cat(sprintf("Tuned keepX per component: %s; %d fragments entered elimination; final panel: %d\n",
            paste(tun$keepX[tapply(seq_len(nrow(tun)), tun$comp, function(i) i[which.max(tun$loso_auc[i])])], collapse = ", "),
            el$n_features[1], utils::tail(el$n_features, 1)))
## Tuned keepX per component: 50, 5; 55 fragments entered elimination; final panel: 2

How to read this:

  • A (training) and B (LOSO, panel fixed) are the two estimates the paper reports (0.89 and 0.78 there). The panel was chosen on the same 25 patients for both, so neither is an independent estimate.
  • The permutation null reruns the same pipeline after flipping BL/M4 labels within random patients, so there is no treatment effect. It still gives training AUCs around 0.96 and LOSO AUCs around 0.94. The observed training AUC sits at permutation p = 0.24 (20 permutations). With about 3,000 fragments, about 25 pairs and within-patient centring, high A and B values are expected even without a real effect. An A or B value alone therefore cannot show that VOCs changed.
  • C (nested CV) is the honest estimate. Use paired accuracy (the share of patients whose 4-month sample scores higher than their baseline sample), not pooled AUC: each fold’s model puts scores on its own scale. The table gives the mean over 5 repeats, with the min–max range in the CI columns. Nested leave-one-subject-out is available (--nested_folds=loso) but is biased downwards when selection is this aggressive (see the skill’s SKILL.md).

Recall of the planted truth. The tuned sPLS-DA model, before elimination, contained 5 of the 5 planted VOCs. The elimination rule then cut it down to the smallest set that keeps the training AUC ≥ 0.9.

8 The published 5-VOC panel as a fixed panel (Fig. 4)

To mirror the paper’s figures for the five compounds it reports, we evaluate that panel directly, with no selection (--panel). In the simulation these are the planted VOCs.

v5 <- truth$feature[truth$type == "time_effect"]
run5 <- "splsda/BLvsM4_breath_voc_paper5"

      c(paste0("--config=", CFG), "--layer=breath_voc", "--visits=BL,M4",
        paste0("--panel=", paste(v5, collapse = ",")), "--plot_visits=BL,M1,M4",
        "--colour_by=biologic", "--tag=paper5"),
      done = file.path(RES, run5, "performance.csv"), show = 0)

11 VOC change by biologic

The paper saw no visual difference in VOC trajectories between biologics. The engine’s existing stats-group-testing skill tests that directly. It compares the change from baseline (M4 − BL) between dupilumab (n = 20) and benralizumab (n = 5) for every fragment, with FDR correction.

skill(file.path(K, "stats-group-testing/scripts/group_tests.R"),
      c(paste0("--config=", CFG), "--design=between", "--by=group", "--visit=M4",
        "--change_from=BL", "--layers=breath_voc"),
      done = file.path(RES, "tests/between_group_M4_minusBL/breath_voc_tests.csv"), show = 0)

13 What the replication shows

  1. The workflow reproduces end to end with engine skills. Three methods were missing and are now skills: breath GC-MS preprocessing, multilevel sPLS-DA with backward elimination and LOSO, and the Kendall / Mann–Whitney / paired-change clinical statistics.
  2. The published validation is optimistic by design. Features were selected once on all patients (stated in the paper), so the LOSO-CV of the fixed panel is not independent. The permutation null shows the pipeline can score highly with no effect. The nested estimate and the re-selection frequencies are the numbers to carry forward to the full 3TR-ABC cohort.
  3. The elimination rule is unstable. “Remove while the AUC drops ≤ 5%” evaluated on the training AUC tends towards one or two features, and which features survive depends on chance. Inside the nested folds it often leaves a single VOC. The skill offers --elim_auc=loso and --target_auc=NA for sensitivity analyses.
  4. Ambiguities in the paper’s methods, with the choices made here (all are skill options): relative vs absolute 5% AUC drop (relative); AUC for elimination (training); number of sPLS-DA components (2); how keepX was tuned (sequential LOSO AUC); CI method for Kendall’s tau (bootstrap); the log base and how zeros were handled (log2, half-minimum); the definition of FEV1 ≥ 10% (percentage points).

13.1 Methods paragraph (template)

Exhaled-breath GC-MS feature tables were processed with the DMP-AE prep-breathomics-gcms skill: known contaminants were removed, intensities were log2-transformed (zeros set to half the fragment minimum) and batch effects were removed with limma::removeBatchEffect, preserving visit. Fragments were z-scored, and within-patient variation was isolated by multilevel decomposition. Sparse PLS-DA (2 components; keepX tuned by leave-one-subject-out AUC) was followed by backward elimination (ml-multilevel-splsda; engine: internal). Performance was estimated by patient-grouped 5-fold cross-validation (5 repeats), with keepX tuning and elimination repeated inside each training fold (nested). Significance was assessed against 20 within-patient label permutations. Clinical changes were tested with paired t or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests according to the Shapiro–Wilk test, and baseline associations with Kendall’s tau (stats-clinical-association).
